tldr: By placing a reinforcement learning policy on top of a model-based whole-body impulse controller (WBIC) to adapt structured reference targets like footholds and contact forces, the authors significantly improved quadruped survival against severe disturbances.
overview:
Quadruped locomotion requires simultaneously coordinating body motion, contact forces, foothold placement, and gait timing. Conventional model-based controllers (such as MPC and WBIC) offer excellent reliability and physical validity, but adapting these parameters flexibly under disturbances is difficult. On the other hand, reinforcement learning that directly outputs joint position targets provides strong adaptability, yet it requires learning coordination from scratch and often suffers from dynamical failures.

To address this, the authors propose a hierarchical architecture where a model-based control backbone—already capable of sustaining a nominal trot—remains in place at the lower level, while an upper-level reinforcement learning policy outputs 25-dimensional structured locomotion references. Training takes place inside a C++ simulation loop (MuJoCo–EnvPool) that incorporates the entire gait scheduler and whole-body impulse controller (WBIC).

In a six-direction disturbance grid evaluation, the proposed method achieved a high disturbance survival rate of 77.29%, compared to just 50.35% for the conventional MPC+WBIC baseline. Furthermore, training-time channel ablation experiments revealed that adaptive foothold placement is the largest marginal contributor to surviving disturbances, while gait-rate adaptation yields direction-dependent effects.
contributions: Proposed a hierarchical architecture where a single reinforcement learning policy jointly adapts body motion, contact forces, foothold placement, body height, and gait cadence.
Constructed a high-speed, parallelized MuJoCo–EnvPool environment that executes the entire control loop—including the whole-body impulse controller (WBIC) and gait scheduler—directly in the loop.
Demonstrated a 77.29% mean survival rate across an exhaustive six-direction disturbance grid up to 5.0 m/s, significantly outperforming the model-based reference controller (50.35%).
Conducted training-time channel ablation experiments that identified adaptive foothold placement as the most critical factor for survival.
Showed that learned structured locomotion references provide a viable pathway to combine learned adaptation with optimization-based whole-body control.

sections.heading: Why combine model-based control with reinforcement learning?
sections.summary: Quadruped locomotion is a complex control problem interleaving continuous body motion and discrete contact switching. This paper presents an approach that merges the reliability of a model-based backbone with the adaptability of reinforcement learning to adjust high-level, physically meaningful reference targets.
sections.details:
Locomotion control for quadruped robots is a hybrid control problem with tightly coupled continuous floating-base dynamics and discrete contact schedule changes. When a disturbance occurs, the robot must rapidly coordinate body posture, ground reaction forces, contact placement, and gait timing all at once within a very short time window.

Traditional model-based control addresses this by decomposing the problem into a hierarchy: gait timing, foothold planning, contact force computation, whole-body control, and joint feedback. For instance, convex MPC plans ground reaction forces, and an optimization-based whole-body controller like WBIC (Whole-Body Impulse Control) maps them into executable joint torques. While this structure offers physical plausibility and interpretability, relying on Raibert heuristics for footholds and fixing the gait cycle limits adaptability to unknown disturbances.

Reinforcement learning (RL), conversely, is a powerful tool for discovering adaptive behaviors through trial and error. However, standard joint-space RL—where the policy directly outputs joint position setpoints—must implicitly learn stable gait coordination from scratch, without guarantees on dynamics or contact constraints.

Rather than replacing the low-level controller with RL, this work retains a model-based backbone capable of an independent nominal trot. The RL policy acts as a supervisor, learning when and how to modify structured references. This frees the learning process from mastering basic limb coordination and lets it focus entirely on the core challenge of disturbance recovery.

sections.heading: Coordinating whole-body control with a 25-dimensional structured action space
sections.summary: The proposed system consists of a learning policy running at 100 Hz, alongside a gait scheduler, reactive footstep planner, and WBIC running at 500 Hz. The policy outputs a 25-dimensional reference vector spanning body velocities, contact force targets, foothold offsets, body height, and gait phase progression.
sections.details:
Here is the overall design and component breakdown of the proposed hierarchical controller:

### II-A Overall Architecture
The control loop is divided into two frequencies. The upper-level learning policy operates at 100 Hz, outputting a 25-dimensional action from a 54-dimensional observation vector. The lower-level model-based stack (gait scheduler, footstep planner, WBIC) runs at 500 Hz, executing the policy's commands over 5 sub-steps (2 ms each) using high-frequency state feedback.

### II-B Policy Formulation and Reward Design
The 25-dimensional action consists of body velocity residuals (3D), contact force targets for each leg ($4 \times 3 = 12$D), horizontal foothold position residuals ($4 \times 2 = 8$D), body height residual (1D), and gait cadence adjustment (1D). Only contact forces are specified as absolute targets; all others act as residuals added to nominal baselines. Observations include base posture, velocities, joint states, and scheduled gait phase, without requiring history buffers or privileged disturbance information. The bounded reward function uses exponential kernels to penalize task-space tracking errors and terminates the episode with a penalty of $-10$ upon falling.

### II-C Continuous Gait Scheduling
The gait is rooted in a nominal trot with a 0.4 s cycle, alternating diagonal leg pairs based on a normalized phase $\theta \in [0, 1)$. The policy modulates gait cadence through its phase rate action, speeding up, slowing down, or pausing phase advancement.

### II-D Footstep Trajectory Planning
Swing leg landing locations add the policy's horizontal foothold residuals to nominal targets computed by a velocity-based Raibert heuristic. Foot trajectories are generated using Bézier curves with a nominal 0.10 m ground clearance.

### II-E Whole-Body Impulse Control (WBIC)
WBIC optimizes body and swing-foot tracking tasks while enforcing floating-base rigid-body dynamics, contact constraints, and friction cones (friction coefficient $\mu=0.45$). The policy's contact force targets serve as regularization reference points in the optimization, which are refined to satisfy physical feasibility and translated into joint torque commands.

sections.heading: A vectorized controller-in-the-loop training setup and disturbance evaluation protocol
sections.summary: The authors developed an EnvPool environment that embeds the full WBIC control loop inside parallel MuJoCo simulations to train the policy with PPO. Evaluation was performed on a Go2 robot across a fine-grained benchmark grid of velocity disturbances spanning 6 directions and 10 intensity levels.
sections.details:
To rigorously evaluate the proposed method, the authors built a specialized training environment and evaluation protocol:

### III-A Vectorized Controller-in-the-Loop Environment
To accelerate training, the MuJoCo simulator and the complete 500 Hz whole-body control stack (WBIC and scheduler) were implemented together in C++ within EnvPool. A key advantage is that the policy trains directly against the unsimplified control loop running in parallel at high throughput.

### III-B Policy Training Setup and Curriculum
The policy was trained using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). The setup used 256 parallel environments collecting rollouts of 512 steps. A curriculum progressively increased the maximum disturbance magnitude through 1 m/s, 2 m/s, and 3 m/s stages over a total of 85 million environment steps.

### III-C Evaluation Protocol and Baselines
A 15 kg Unitree Go2 model was used for testing (Figure F2). The evaluation protocol applied instantaneous base velocity disturbances across 6 directions (forward, backward, left, right, upward, downward) in 0.5 m/s increments up to 5.0 m/s, yielding a 60-cell grid. Each condition was evaluated over 100 trials, assessing whether the robot could survive 5.5 seconds post-disturbance without falling. Baselines included an MIT Mini-Cheetah-derived convex MPC+WBIC stack and a standard joint-space RL recipe, both evaluated under the exact same simulation protocol.

### III-D Training-Time Action Channel Ablations
To measure the individual contribution of each component in the 25-dimensional action space, ablation experiments were designed where specific action channels were disabled (clamped to neutral baselines) and retrained from scratch.

captions.F2: The Unitree Go2 robot in the simulation environment under disturbance evaluation. Blue arrows indicate the disturbance directions applied as instantaneous body velocity impulses during locomotion.

sections.heading: Achieving 77.3% survival rate, with foothold adaptation leading the way
sections.summary: The proposed method achieved a 77.29% mean survival rate across the disturbance grid, substantially surpassing the 50.35% rate of MPC+WBIC. Ablation studies revealed that foothold adaptation contributes the most to overall survival, while gait-rate adaptation has direction-dependent effects.
sections.details:
The experimental evaluation produced several key findings:

### IV-A Training Stability
Across three independent seeds, training completed 85 million steps without divergence, reaching episode timeout rates (surviving without falling) between 92.9% and 98.4%. This highlights that the complex hierarchical architecture trains reliably.

### IV-B Disturbance Grid Survival Comparison
In nominal conditions without disturbances, all controllers achieved 100% survival. Across the 60-cell disturbance grid, however, the proposed controller achieved a 77.29% mean survival rate (averaged across three seeds), outperforming the baseline MPC+WBIC (50.35%) by 26.94 percentage points (the reference joint-space RL baseline achieved 54.01%). Lateral robustness saw massive gains: the 50% survival threshold ($c_{50}$) nearly doubled from 2.26 m/s to 4.19 m/s for leftward pushes, and from 1.96 m/s to 3.80 m/s for rightward pushes. Under backward impulses, the robot maintained a 70.3% survival rate even at the maximum 5.0 m/s limit, exceeding the measurable grid range.

### IV-C Ablation Analysis of Action Channels
As shown in Figure F5, retraining the policy with individual action groups disabled revealed that removing foothold residuals caused the sharpest drop in grid survival, falling from 77.43% to 66.60% (a $-10.83$ percentage point drop). The degradation was most pronounced in lateral directions, proving that active foot placement is essential for brace-and-catch maneuvers. Interestingly, removing foothold residuals slightly improved downward disturbance survival, revealing directional trade-offs. Similarly, fixing gait cadence reduced upward push survival but slightly improved backward push resistance, demonstrating distinct directional roles across channels.

### IV-D Nominal Locomotion Efficiency
Analyzing unperturbed flat-ground walking revealed that policies trained with fixed cadence or fixed footholds exhibited lower joint torque RMS and lower Cost of Transport (CoT). The active footstep and cadence adjustments learned for disturbance recovery introduce a functional trade-off, sacrificing slight nominal efficiency for superior recovery robustness.

captions.F5: Results of training-time action channel ablations. The left chart shows overall grid survival drops (removing foothold residuals causes the largest drop at 10.83 percentage points), while the right heatmap displays shifts in the 50% survival threshold $c_{50}$ across disturbance directions, highlighting the decisive role of foothold adaptation against lateral disturbances.

sections.heading: Adaptability through hierarchy, and open questions for hardware deployment
sections.summary: This work demonstrates the effectiveness of learning structured high-level references while retaining an optimization-based low-level controller. While promising, future work must explore real-robot deployment, rough terrain generalization, and inter-channel compensatory mechanisms.
sections.details:
The results demonstrate that stacking a reinforcement learning adaptation layer over a model-based whole-body controller (WBIC) is a practical and potent architecture.

Importantly, the authors do not claim that their method is intrinsically superior to joint-space RL under all conditions. The baseline joint-space RL's moderate survival rate was largely due to its recipe not being tailored to this aggressive disturbance curriculum; with equivalent tuning, joint-space RL might achieve comparable robustness. The core takeaway is architectural: high-frequency dynamics can remain safely handled by an interpretable model-based foundation, while physically grounded reference modulation delivers remarkable disturbance adaptability.

Another key insight from the ablations is inter-channel compensation. Even without foothold residuals, the policy retained a 66.60% survival rate, indicating that other channels like body velocity and contact force adaptation step in to partially shoulder the burden.

Several limitations remain. Evaluations were conducted on flat ground in simulation using instantaneous velocity impulses; sustained external forces, large rotational perturbations, and rough terrain navigation were not investigated. Moreover, although WBIC has an extensive track record on physical hardware, direct sim-to-real transfer of this learned hierarchical policy has yet to be demonstrated.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future outlook
sections.summary: The authors proposed a hierarchical locomotion controller where reinforcement learning adapts structured reference targets, achieving a 77.29% disturbance survival rate in simulation. Foothold adaptation proved to be the cornerstone of robust recovery, highlighting a clear path forward for combining model-based control with learning.
sections.details:
This paper presented a hierarchical quadruped controller where a gait scheduler, reactive footstep planner, and WBIC manage high-frequency whole-body execution, while a reinforcement learning policy coordinates structured references for body motion, contact forces, foothold placement, body height, and gait timing.

In extensive simulation disturbance grids, the proposed controller achieved a 77.29% mean survival rate, markedly exceeding the 50.35% baseline achieved by traditional model-based control. Training-time ablations confirmed that adaptive foothold placement is the single largest marginal contributor to surviving disturbances, and gait-rate modulation provides direction-dependent recovery benefits.

Future work will focus on testing the architecture across diverse terrains, evaluating behavior under noisy state estimation, and validating the framework through real-world hardware transfer experiments.

takeaways: Preserving the model-based low-level controller (WBIC) and using RL to modulate physically meaningful 25-dimensional references yields high disturbance robustness without training instability.
Integrating the full model-based control loop directly inside a vectorized C++ simulation environment (EnvPool) enables fast, end-to-end parallel reinforcement learning.
Adaptive foothold placement is the single most dominant factor in recovering from severe disturbances, while gait cadence adaptation helps manage direction-dependent resilience.
Rather than pitting RL against model-based control, establishing a clean division of labor between high-level adaptation and low-level execution provides a compelling paradigm for legged locomotion.
limitations: Evaluations are restricted to flat-ground simulation; performance on challenging uneven terrains, such as stairs or slopes, remains untested.
Disturbances were primarily modeled as instantaneous translational velocity impulses, leaving responses to continuous external forces or heavy rotational moments unexamined.
Sim-to-real hardware experiments on the Go2 robot were not conducted, leaving the effects of physical modeling errors and sensing latency as open questions.
